defects: Staging build: 3 of 10 trading days of history so far; the call needs 10 trading days of scores before it can be confirmed.
Valuation vs own history (VL3) uses trailing P/E: free forward P/E history is too short.

VL3's 5-year P/E median (87.3x) is overstated: the collector derives fourth-quarter EPS as full year minus three quarters, which goes wrong across stock splits (Q4 FY Jan 2022 shows −$1.09 instead of $1.18; Q4 FY Jan 2025 −$4.49 instead of $0.89). The first inflates 2022-23 P/Es, the second drops about a year of lower readings. With corrected EPS the median is about 55-57x and today's 30.0x is about 45-47% below it: still bullish. The median also reflects depressed 2022-23 earnings, so 'cheap vs history' carries little information. Framework fix pending.
EV/EBITDA uses last-12-month EBITDA (free source); three of the five peers fall outside the 2x-80x range, so the peer median rests on Broadcom and Arista.
Chain C2 watches Micron's share price as a stand-in for memory prices.
DM4a deliberately measures growth vs the prior quarter, not vs a year earlier (Kenneth, 5 Oct 2026), to catch a slowdown sooner.
Revenue mix: Nvidia reports profit only for its Compute & Networking and Graphics segments, which do not match Data Center and Edge Computing, so both parts show the whole-company margin.

A $400m provision on excess H200 inventory (10-Q, first half of FY27) is not removed from DM6 because its split between quarters is not disclosed; removing it would raise the latest margin by about 0.1 point.
Trailing GAAP earnings include $23.7bn of first-half gains on equity holdings, so the trailing P/E (30.0x) understates the operating P/E (about 34x without them).

DM4a, DM4b and DM5 are entered by hand at each results date (Nvidia CFO commentary; cloud companies' reports). DM5 mixes bases: Alphabet reports cash capex only, the others include finance leases; Microsoft's change to data-centre asset lives will distort future comparisons.

One driver: price trend, Demand and Valuation all depend on the AI capex cycle and the FY28 consensus ($15.91); the driver cap does not bite when every input is bullish, so 'High' confidence overstates how much independent evidence there is.

Not scored: customers' own chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium), power and grid delays to data-centre build-outs, memory prices (HBM reported up to +50% in 2027), and a low P/E on possibly peak earnings. The 5-year replay found the score did not separate good from bad entry days for NVDA (research/sanity_check.md).

DC.sells: AI accelerators (GPUs and full rack systems such as Blackwell and Vera Rubin), the CPUs and networking that link them, and software.
DC.buyers: The big clouds (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle: 'Hyperscale', about 55% of Data Center in the July quarter) and AI clouds, AI labs, sovereign and corporate buyers ('ACIE', about 45%).
pos: Grew 117% in the July quarter vs a year earlier; the fastest-growing part.
Sold as complete systems with networking and software, which makes customers stickier and supports a 75% company gross margin.
Demand is broadening: ACIE grew 138% vs a year earlier.
neg: Not contracted recurring revenue: it depends on customers' capex budgets, which are cyclical.
A handful of direct customers buy most of it (one was 16% of company revenue in the July quarter).
Several of the biggest buyers design their own chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium) with Broadcom and Marvell.
China Data Center sales are near zero (under 1% of Data Center revenue in the July quarter); China in total was about 13% of company revenue in the year to Jan 2025.
Part of the demand is financed by Nvidia itself: guarantees of up to $105bn on a data-centre campus leased to OpenAI, and $47.9bn of stakes in unlisted companies, many of them AI customers.

EDGE.sells: Gaming GPUs, professional workstations, chips for cars and robots, PCs and AI-RAN telecom equipment.
EDGE.buyers: Gamers and PC makers, designers and engineers, carmakers and robot builders, telecom operators.
pos: Grew 27% in the July quarter vs a year earlier.
Spreads Nvidia's platform into PCs, cars and robots, a longer-dated growth option.
neg: Small: under a tenth of revenue.
Consumer PC sales slowed as memory made PCs dearer (Nvidia, Q2 FY27).

shift.title: What the shift means for Nvidia
pos: Data Center rose from 67% of sales to 92% in 3 years (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters to Jul 2023), and company gross margin rose from 64.6% to 74.7% over the same period: the AI systems business carries the margin.
Data Center sales grew 90% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters before; Edge Computing grew 35%.
Free cash flow (operating cash minus capital spending) was $127.0bn over the last 12 months to Jul 2026.
neg: Concentration has risen: over nine-tenths of sales now depend on data-centre capex budgets that can be cut quickly.
The biggest buyers are also building alternatives (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium), so share of their spend is not guaranteed.
Margin is guided down 1 point for the October quarter (74.0% vs 75.0%) on memory costs.

move.headline: A small dip from a record close, in line with the market

evidence.t: Nvidia fell 0.7% to $237.47, just under its record close of $239.24 on 6 Oct, while the S&P 500 fell 0.2%. That is within Nvidia's normal daily range (2.3% typical), so no classification is triggered.
Foxconn, which assembles Nvidia's AI servers, reported record September revenue of NT$1.16tn (about $36.5bn), +38% vs a year earlier; TSMC (+3%) and Broadcom (+2%) also rose.
Nvidia added $150bn to its buyback authorisation, about $235bn in total, to be used through FY2028.
The stock is up about 27% this year and about 25% from its 29 Jul low of $190.

lead: Nvidia is Building history (today's zone: Strong Buy), at +89 on a −100 to +100 scale, up from +82 on 6 Oct because its 3-month lead over its peers widened (price trend score +100, from +72): every demand and valuation read is still positive, but the cheapness rests on forecasts that rose 25% in 90 days, and cash is lagging profit.
bullets: Demand is as strong as the framework can read it. Demand scores +100: revenue grew 105.9% in the July quarter vs a year earlier, against a 69.1% average for the prior four quarters; Data Center sales +18.3% vs the April quarter (bullish line +10%); ACIE +138.1% vs a year earlier; consensus EPS for the year to Jan 2028 $15.91 vs $12.71 90 days ago (+25.2%); October-quarter guidance +6.7 points of growth above consensus; big-4 cloud capex about +79% vs a year earlier; gross margin 74.7% over the last 4 quarters vs 72.5% a year earlier (one-off H20 items removed).

Cheap vs peers and its own history, if the forecasts hold. Valuation scores +100: 17.2x next-12-month earnings vs a 45.5x peer median (−62%), though only 14% below Broadcom's 19.9x; growth-adjusted P/E 0.3 vs 0.8 (−64%); EV/EBITDA 28.4x vs 45.4x (−38%, two peers only); trailing P/E 30.0x vs its own 5-year median of 87.3x (−66%; overstated, see Known defects). The discount depends on forecasts that rose 25% in 90 days.

Money flows are mixed. Liquidity scores +27: volume on up days was 2.20x volume on down days over the last 20 trading days (bullish), but the dollar index rose 2.99 points vs 20 trading days earlier (bearish); short interest (1.3% of float), institutional holdings (+1.0 point of shares, just under the +1 line) and Fed odds (rate-rise odds 16% vs 31% four weeks earlier) are neutral.

The price trend is strong again. Price trend scores +100, up from +72: the close was $237.47 (−0.74% on the day vs −0.22% for the S&P 500, a little under the record close of $239.24 on 6 Oct), 17.7% above its 200-day average; the 50-day average is 9.4% above the 200-day; over 3 months Nvidia is 9.7 points ahead of its five peers, up from 4.5 points and above the +5 point line for a bullish read.

What could go wrong. Gross margin is guided down to 74.0% from 75.0% on memory costs; operating cash flow fell to $24.1bn in the July quarter from $50.3bn in April as customers took longer to pay (60 days of sales vs 45); supply commitments rose to $279bn from $119bn a quarter earlier; one customer was 16% of revenue; Nvidia guarantees up to $105bn of a customer's data-centre leases; and the 10-year yield rose to 5.28% from 4.84% a month earlier (chain C3 Active). The call is not confirmed yet: 3 of the 10 trading days needed are recorded, and today reads Strong Buy. Next tests: US inflation 14 Oct and the Fed 28 Oct (C3), TSMC results 15 Oct, big-4 cloud capex in late October (DM5) and Nvidia's results, estimated 17 Nov (DM3, DM4a).
